query: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets provide 16 candidate alloys, nine of which are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing. Early reports associated increasing constituent count with greater strength, but that simple relationship is no longer generally accepted. Despite extensive experimental and theoretical investigation, the origins of differences in deformation and failure behavior remain unresolved; practical interpretation must also account for constituent cost and overall cost-performance balance. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs these mechanical-property differences and why? Define a controlled investigation, the observations predicted relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, the prior evidence supporting it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Local fluctuations in chemical composition—particularly enrichment or depletion of elements like Ni and Mn at dislocation cores and stacking fault interfaces—modulate the stacking fault energy (SFE) in FCC single‐phase and dual‐phase HEAs, thereby tuning which deformation mechanisms (dislocation slip, twinning, or TRIP) are activated. Alloys engineered to exhibit controlled local chemical heterogeneities will initiate deformation twinning and/or phase transformation (TRIP) at lower global strains and achieve a higher work‐hardening rate relative to a chemically homogeneous equiatomic Cantor alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni (Cantor) alloy exhibiting a single-phase FCC microstructure with a relatively uniform elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Introduce controlled microalloying or processing modifications (e.g., minor additions of Al/C or tailored thermomechanical treatments) that promote localized enrichment of Ni (or depletion of Mn) at defect sites without significantly altering the overall composition.
generation.conditions: Prepare and thermomechanically process samples such that the grain sizes, overall phase fractions, and bulk compositions remain similar. Perform mechanical tests (tensile testing) at room temperature and use in situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to observe dislocation behavior and twin nucleation under comparable strain rates.
generation.structural_mediator: Spatial variations in the local stacking fault energy arising from non‐uniform elemental segregation at dislocation cores and stacking fault interfaces.
generation.mechanism: Local elemental variations alter the Gibbs free energy difference between the FCC matrix and potential twin or martensitic phases by changing the local SFE. Regions with lower SFE (e.g. due to higher Ni enrichment) facilitate the dissociation of dislocations into partials and promote early twinning or transformation induced plasticity (TRIP), which in turn enhances work hardening and delays necking.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline equiatomic alloy, samples with deliberately induced local chemical heterogeneities will begin forming deformation twins (and/or show TRIP activity) at lower macroscopic strains, display a higher dislocation density plateau with more pronounced twin and stacking fault networks, and ultimately demonstrate an improved combination of yield strength and ductility due to the synergistic hardening effect of these mechanisms.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni Cantor alloy with uniformly distributed elements and standard thermomechanical processing.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to FCC single-phase or dual-phase high-entropy alloys with similar overall compositions and thermomechanical histories. Extreme changes in alloy chemistry or processing (e.g., conditions that lead to phase separation or entirely different crystal structures) may lie outside its valid regime.
generation.uncertainty: The proposal builds on observations of strong local chemical fluctuations affecting dislocation behavior (PMC7012927::web::017::variations_in_local_chemical_environment) and the documented impact of Al and C additions on SFE and deformation mechanisms (PMC5793551::web::003::1_introduction). The new aspect is the deliberate engineering of spatial chemical heterogeneities to tune SFE and deformation mode activation. Quantitative relationships between the degree of local segregation and the precise SFE change remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same base alloy composition. One set is processed via the standard route to obtain a baseline equiatomic alloy with a uniform elemental distribution. The other set is processed with a controlled addition of minor alloying elements or with a modified heat-treatment schedule designed to promote localized Ni (or Mn) segregation, but maintaining the same global composition. Conduct identical tensile tests while performing in situ TEM observations to monitor dislocation activity, twin formation, and phase transformation. Use analytical techniques (e.g., nano-EDS mapping, atom probe tomography) to verify the presence and spatial distribution of local chemical variations.
measurements: Quantification of local SFE (via dislocation partial separation measurements)
Onset strain for twinning or TRIP activity via in situ TEM
Tensile yield strength and work-hardening rate
Spatial chemical mapping (EDS, APT) to confirm local segregation differences
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the engineered alloys with induced local chemical heterogeneities do not exhibit a statistically significant decrease in the strain for twin or TRIP initiation, a higher work-hardening rate, or improved yield strength/ductility compared to the baseline homogeneous alloy under identical processing and testing conditions, then the hypothesis that local chemical fluctuations modulate deformation mechanisms through SFE variations would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: However, modifications of the chemical composition of the fcc solid solution can also result in changes of different strengthening mechanisms activity. For example, intensive deformation twinning in the CoCrFeNiMn alloy was usually ascribed to a considerable decrease in the stacking fault energy (SFE) values to 20–30 mJ·m−2 [,]; an increase in the SFE values due to alloying can result in twinning suppression that inevitably would have a pronounced effect on the mechanical behavior of the alloys. It has been established earlier that Al and C in austenitic (fcc) steels are among the elements that strongly increase the SFE, thereby promoting dislocation slip and suppressing twinning [,,]. However, there are contradicting reports on the effect of carbon doping on deformation mechanisms operating in the Co-Cr-Fe-Ni-Mn system high entropy alloys [,,,]. The effect of Al is even much less studied, however, deformation twinning was reported for the Al0.1CoCrFeNi alloy, nominally containing ~2.4 at % of Al [,]. Therefore, additional studies on the effects of alloying on deformation mechanisms of the CoCrFeNiMn-type alloys are required.

In this work, over 15 sites were investigated; it is suggested that at the core of the partial dislocations where the SFs end, the concentration of one element significantly increases, while the exact local compositions may vary case by case. For instance, in Fig. 5a, the local chemical environment in this sub-nanometer region was found to be enriched in Ni. It is worth noting that although this dual-phase HEA contains the same five elements as the Cantor alloy, the fluctuation in local concentration of elements is much higher. It is also reasoned that there is larger lattice distortion in the dual-phase HEA Cr20Mn6Fe34Co34Ni6 than in the Cantor alloy, with the increase in Co and Fe content and reduction in Mn and Ni content.
